doc.title: Jim Galloway interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Sidney Bechet and the emotional impact of live playing
summary: Grove compares him to Bechet; Galloway recalls seeing Bechet live, the intensity of his playing, and similar magic in Louis Armstrong.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Did you know that you have a pretty nice entry in the Grove Dictionary?
I know there’s an entry in there. I don’t have the book but I know there’s an entry.
One thing they say is, “plays soprano sax in a lyrical style reminiscent of Sidney Bechet.”

Well I guess anybody who has ever decided to play soprano sax, if they’re at all aware of the origins of the music, they have to have heard Bechet. He was, after all, he was the first great saxophone soloist in jazz. Statement made. And I don’t think I particularly played like him, but you absorb influences and certainly he’s in there. I listened a lot to him. I saw him once live, when he toured in Britain obviously before I left, and I was transfixed by his playing. The hairs on the back of my neck actually stood up, and I walked out of that concert totally changed. It was a tremendous emotional impact of his playing which you just cannot capture on record, no matter how great the records might be, just the experience of having heard him in the flesh, woah, it blew me away. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Was he playing only soprano then or was he playing a clarinet at all?
No he was playing soprano then. And of course a straight one.
The straight one. Well that’s quite a statement. Can you describe what it was about his playing that had such an emotional impact?

Oh, there’s an intensity to it, and actually this is interesting, his centennial was last year, and I’d been invited to New Orleans to be part of a panel discussion, and play in the street parade. And one of the things that I commented on, because I think he doesn’t receive perhaps the recognition that he could have, and I think in a sense it may have been because, and this is only a little theory of mine, but when he played, he really pierced your emotions. And that can be uncomfortable for a lot of people. And I know that to me he just here, he just got right in here, and as I say, like that, and it was the intensity of his playing, he was a marvelous harmonic player, and he had a wonderful harmonic concept, and great lines. And a lot of people found that high vibrato a little difficult to take but even if you do, if you listen beyond that, what the guy was playing, it was so powerful. And I mean I had the same experience hearing Louis Armstrong. And for me just to hear Louis play a middle C, I mean it was magic. So those sort of things, they stay with you, and obviously they leave their mark. I think that emotional aspect of the music is so important. For me it’s the difference between a good wine and a glass of plonk, that magic thing that was there. And the great ones have it.
